game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Four dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 3, 3, 5, 5, 10, 11.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 12.
- Die 4 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 3, 5, 9, 10.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 2, 4 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 6, 4 cards worth 7, 4 cards worth 11, 4 cards worth 15. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
My estimate of the settlement value is about 8, well below the unconditional mean of 13.8, so I'm quoting around that with a wide spread and a slight lean toward selling since I'm already long.

- **Prior:** the deck's 22 cards sum to 152, so the mean card is about 6.9 and the unconditional mean of two cards is about 13.8.
- **Update from the trade:** a counterparty sold to me at 6.8. A noise trader would do that with probability about 0.13. An informed trader would do it when the sum is 6 or less, which has probability 40/231, about 0.17. The sale therefore makes it more likely I faced an informed seller, and in that case the value is low (mean about 3.4).
- **Posterior:** the chance that the last trader was informed is about 0.55, and the posterior mean of the settlement value is about 8.
- **Quote:** the posterior is bimodal and about half the next arrivals are likely informed, so I quote wide around 8 and lean the ask slightly lower to work off my long position.

I'm already long one unit, so I lean slightly toward selling.

Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.

|---|---|

| 12 | 0.0625 |
| 13 | 0.375 |
| 14 | 0.0625 |
| 18 | 0.125 |

- An informed trader costs me E[(V − 13 − d)+] on each trade.
- At d = 1 the informed losses (about 0.54) far exceed the noise profit (about 0.20).
- At d = 3 the two roughly cancel.
- At d = 5 the expected edge peaks at about 0.11 per side, because only the 19 outcome is still in the money for an informed buyer.

Since this is the last quote, I only need to maximise expected profit on this one trade. I weighed the noise trader's trading chance against the loss to an informed trader, assuming alpha is around 0.4.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 15 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 3, 1 card worth 4, 3 cards worth 6, 1 card worth 7, 2 cards worth 9, 3 cards worth 11, 4 cards worth 12. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
I'm quoting a wide spread because alpha is unknown and an informed trader would pick off a narrow one.

With card 1 = 12, the other 14 cards are 3, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12. They average 8.5, so the settlement value is 20.5 on average. The possible settlements are 15, 16, 18 (×3), 19, 21 (×2), 23 (×3) and 24 (×3).

I compared candidate quotes by expected profit, averaged over alpha ∈ {0.05, 0.5, 0.9}. For each quote I added the noise-trader gain, using valuation ~ N(20.5, 3.5), and the informed-trader loss.

- **Ask:** at 24.0 an informed buyer never has an edge, since the highest settlement is 24, while noise traders still buy about 16% of the time. A lower ask such as 22.5 loses more to informed buyers than it gains from noise traders at high alpha. I chose 24.0.
- **Bid:** at 16.0 an informed seller has no edge either, since the lowest settlement is 15 and a seller at 16 only breaks even. Noise traders sell about 10% of the time. I chose 16.0.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 24.0}

Card 1 is 12, so the remaining 14 cards are 3, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12. Their mean is 119/14 ≈ 8.5, so the public fair value is about 20.5. The possible settlement values are 15, 16, 18, 18, 18, 19, 21, 21, 23, 23, 23, 24, 24, 24.

- **Ask 24:** The highest possible settlement value is 24, so an informed buyer never pays more than 24 for a contract worth less. A noise trader buys with probability about 16% and I earn about 3.5 on each such sale. Lower asks such as 23 or 23.5 bring in more noise flow but lose to informed buyers when alpha is high.
- **Bid 16:** An informed seller only gains from me when the value is 15, a 1-in-14 chance with a loss of 1. A noise trader sells with probability about 10% and I earn about 4.5 on each such purchase. Bids of 15.5 and 17 average slightly lower once the informed-trader risk is counted.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 24}

My fair value for the sum is about 17.5. The deck's 15 cards total 131, so the average card is about 8.73 and two cards average about 17.47. The sum has a standard deviation of roughly 4.1, so an informed trader could be well on either side of the mean. I'm quoting about ±1.9 around fair value, which earns a decent edge from noise traders while limiting losses to informed ones.

{"bid": 15.6, "ask": 19.4}

With card 1 = 6, the 14 remaining cards average 125/14 ≈ 8.93, so the fair value of the settlement is about 14.9. The possible settlement values are 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 17 and 18. An informed buyer only profits at my ask if the value is 17 or 18, and an informed seller only profits at my bid if the value is 12 or below.

I checked a few levels against a mixed informed/noise population (alpha around 0.5):

- **Ask:** about 17.8 gives roughly the best expected edge. It is above every value except 18, so informed buyers rarely hit it, and noise traders still pay a large margin over fair value.
- **Bid:** around 11.5 to 12 gives a small positive edge. Lower bids are safer against informed sellers. I'm already long 1, so I'm not pushing to buy more.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 17.8}

Card 1 is 6, so the 14 remaining cards have a mean of 125/14 ≈ 8.93. The public fair value is therefore about 14.93.

An informed buyer only profits if card 2 is 12, which makes the settlement 18. An ask of 18.0 loses nothing to informed buyers, since they need a valuation strictly above the ask. Noise buyers still take it about 19% of the time.

On the bid side, informed sellers hold settlements of 9 or 10 in the worst cases. A bid near 11 limits that loss while still catching noise sellers.

{"bid": 11.0, "ask": 18.0}

Card 1 is 4, so card 2 comes from the remaining 14 cards. Their values sum to 127, a mean of about 9.07. The public fair value is therefore about 13.07.

An informed trader knows card 2, so the settlement value is one of 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 or 16. Those occur with probabilities 1/14, 3/14, 1/14, 2/14, 3/14 and 4/14.

I scored candidate quotes at an assumed alpha of 0.5. I mixed the informed trader's expected loss with the noise trader's expected gain, using noise valuations of fair value plus Normal noise with standard deviation 3.5.

- **Ask:** At 14 the expected profit is negative, and at 15 it is only slightly positive. At 16 an informed buyer never profits, and a noise buyer arrives with probability about 0.20 at a margin of about 2.9. I chose 16.
- **Bid:** At 10 an informed seller at value 7 costs more than the noise gain offsets. At 9 an informed seller never profits, and a noise seller arrives with probability about 0.12 at a margin of about 4. I chose 9.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 16}

Card 1 is 4, so the remaining 14 cards are 3, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12. Their mean is about 9.07, so the public fair value is about 13.07. The settlement value is 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 or 16, with probabilities 1/14, 3/14, 1/14, 2/14, 3/14 and 4/14.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only profits against me if the value is above my ask. The most the value can be is 16, so an ask of 15.6 only loses to informed buyers when the value is 16, and then only 0.4. Noise traders buy about a quarter of the time at a price well above fair value, so this ask has a clear positive expected profit.

**Bid:** At a bid of 10, an informed seller only profits against me when the value is 7, and I lose 3 in that case. Noise traders sell about 19% of the time, and each sale is worth about 3 to me in expectation. This is positive in expectation.

My position is short 1, so a bid near 10 also helps move me back toward flat.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 15.6}

Card 1 is 6, so card 2 comes from the 14 remaining cards: 3, 4, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12. Their mean is about 8.93, so the public fair value is about 14.9 and the settlement ranges from 9 to 18.

I weighed the expected profit of several ask and bid levels, averaging over the three possible alpha values:

- **Ask:** At 16, informed buyers (values 17 and 18) cost more than the noise buyers pay in. At about 17.3, only the value-18 informed buyers cost anything, and the noise trade still earns a good margin.
- **Bid:** Expected profit is roughly flat between 11 and 12.5. I'll bid 12, which sits slightly toward the middle given I'm already long 1.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 17.3}

Card 1 is 6, so the final sum is 6 plus a card drawn from the 14 left: 3, 4, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12. Their mean is about 8.93, so the prior fair value is about 14.9.

The last trade, a counterparty selling to me at 12, pulls that down. An informed seller would only sell below 12 if the other card were 3 or 4, and a noise seller is more likely when the true value is lower. Mixing over the three possible alpha values, I estimate fair value at about 12.7.

I am long 2, so I want to lean slightly toward selling. I keep the spread wide because an informed buyer would hit a tight ask when the sum is 15, 17 or 18, and an informed seller would hit a tight bid when it is 9 or 10. I set the bid at 11.2 and the ask at 14.2.

{"bid": 11.2, "ask": 14.2}

The public fair value is about 17.5, the mean sum of two cards from the deck (131/15 × 2 ≈ 17.47). The buy at 19.3 tells me little: an informed buyer would need a sum above 19.3, which happens about 1/3 of the time, and a noise buyer would also buy about 30% of the time. So I move my fair value up only slightly, to about 17.6. I'm short one unit, so I lean a little toward buying, keeping a wide spread against informed traders.

{"bid": 15.9, "ask": 19.4}

Card 1 is 11, so the remaining 14 cards are 3, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12. They average about 8.57, which puts public fair value near 19.6. The settlement value is 11 plus card 2, so it can only be 14, 15, 17, 18, 20, 22 or 23.

An informed trader only trades against me when I'm on the wrong side of the true value. Hitting my ask costs me most when the value is 22 or 23, and hitting my bid costs me most when it is 14 or 15. I assumed alpha around 0.5, the average of the three possible values. On that assumption, expected profit per arrival is highest with the ask near 22 and the bid near 16.

- **Ask at 22:** it only loses to an informed buyer when the value is 23, and noise traders buy about 24% of the time at a gain of about 2.4.
- **Bid at 16:** it only loses to an informed seller when the value is 14 or 15, and noise traders sell about 15% of the time at a gain of about 3.6.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 22}

Card 1 is 11, so card 2 comes from the 14 remaining cards: 3, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12. Their mean is about 8.57, so the fair value is about 19.57.

An informed buyer would only take my ask when card 2 is 11 or 12 (settlement 22 or 23). An informed seller would only hit my bid when the settlement is 18 or lower. I compared the noise-trader gain against the informed-trader loss at alpha of about 0.5.

- **Ask:** the edge is best around 22.3. Below that, informed buyers cost too much. Above it, noise traders rarely buy.
- **Bid:** the edge is best around 15.5 to 16. I'll use 16.

I'm short one unit, but being risk-neutral I don't skew the quotes for that.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 22.3}

The public fair value is the expected sum of two cards from the 15-card deck. The deck totals 131, so the mean card is 8.73 and the expected sum is about 17.47. The standard deviation of the sum is about 4.15, a bit above the noise traders' 3.5. Nothing is revealed yet and my position is 0, so I'll quote symmetrically around 17.5 with a spread of about 1.7 on each side. That is close to my earlier quotes and still covers the adverse-selection risk from informed traders.

{"bid": 15.8, "ask": 19.2}

I'm short one unit with cash of 19.2, and card 1 is 4. The 14 remaining cards are 3, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12, which sum to 127. The expected value of card 2 is therefore about 9.07, so the public fair value is about 13.07.

An informed trader would know card 2 exactly. The settlement value would then be one of 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 or 16, with 16 the most likely at 4/14. I assumed alpha of about 0.5 and compared expected profit across ask and bid levels.

- **Ask:** profit is highest around 16. At 14 an informed buyer costs me too much, and above about 17 the noise-trader fill rate falls off.
- **Bid:** profit is flat between about 9.5 and 10. A bid near 9.8 collects noise-trader sells at a good edge and limits losses to an informed seller holding the 7.

I'm quoting both sides, since being short from 19.2 is already favourable against a fair value near 13.

{"bid": 9.8, "ask": 16.0}

Card 1 is 4, so the settlement value is 4 plus card 2. The 14 unseen cards are 3, 6×3, 7, 9×2, 11×3 and 12×4. Card 2 has an expected value of about 9.07, so the fair value is about 13.07. The possible settlement values are 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 and 16.

The trade at 16 and the earlier trade at 19.2 were noise traders, not informed ones. Both prices were at or above the maximum possible value of 16, so an informed trader would not have bought there. Those trades say nothing about card 2.

For the last quote I used alpha = 0.5 as a middle case. I picked the prices that maximise the expected profit on each side.

- **Ask at 16:** The ask cannot lose to an informed buyer, because no value exceeds 16. A noise trader buys with probability about 0.20, and I gain about 2.9 per trade.
- **Bid at 10:** An informed seller only trades if the value is 7, which happens 1 time in 14, and that costs me about 3. A noise trader sells with probability about 0.19, and I gain about 3.1 per trade. This beats a bid of 11 (expected profit about 0.04 versus 0.185 for 10) and a bid of 7 (about 0.126).

{"bid": 10, "ask": 16}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 6, 10.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 4, 9, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
I priced this from the distribution of the largest of the three dice.

Each die's CDF at the relevant breakpoints gives P(max ≤ x) as the product of the three. The resulting probabilities for the maximum are:

| Max value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | 0.028 |
| 4 | 0.014 |
| 5 | 0.083 |
| 6 | 0.0625 |
| 8 | 0.0625 |
| 9 | 0.167 |
| 10 | 0.25 |
| 12 | 0.333 |

The expected settlement value is about 9.43.

Informed counterparties are the main risk. If alpha is high, they buy from me when the max is 12, which happens a third of the time. They sell to me when the max is low, and I would lose roughly 3 on those trades. I therefore quote a wide spread around 9.43 rather than a tight one. Noise traders, with valuation noise of 2.1, still trade often enough at this width to give me edge.

{"bid": 8.4, "ask": 10.4}

Die 3 is 12, and no other die can exceed 10, so the contract settles at exactly 12. The fair value is therefore 12, and an informed trader's valuation is also 12. That means an informed trader will never buy from me above 12 or sell to me below 12, so quotes on the right side of 12 face only noise traders.

Against a noise trader, a quote at distance x from 12 earns x per fill and fills with probability 1 − Φ(x/2.1). Maximising x·(1 − Φ(x/2.1)) gives x ≈ 1.5, so I quote symmetrically around 12:

- Ask 13.5: any fill sells at 1.5 above the settlement value.
- Bid 10.5: any fill buys at 1.5 below the settlement value.

I'm at −2, so I can sell one more unit or buy up to +3 without hitting a limit.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is about 9.43, the mean of the maximum of the three dice. The maximum is 12 with probability 1/3, 10 with 1/4 and 9 with 1/6. It is 8 or lower with probability 1/4.

Informed counterparties are a risk, and alpha is unknown. They buy whenever the maximum exceeds my ask, and the maximum is 12 a third of the time. A wide, high ask therefore protects me, while noise traders with SD 2.1 still pay it occasionally.

- **Ask 11.9:** informed buyers cost almost nothing, since the maximum is at most 12. Noise traders buy about 12% of the time at a margin of roughly 2.5. This is positive in expectation at every alpha I'm considering.
- **Bid 6.0:** informed sellers appear only when the maximum is 3 to 5, which is rare, and the expected loss is small. Noise traders sell about 5% of the time at a margin of roughly 3.4. This is roughly break-even at alpha 0.5.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 11.9}

The contract settles at the max of three dice. Working out its distribution gives a prior mean of about 9.43.

- **Evidence on the hidden state:** Someone just bought at 11.9. Only die 3 = 12 (probability 1/3) can make the settlement exceed about 10. The earlier buys at about 10.4 were consistent with high informed-trader activity, so alpha is probably high. That makes die 3 = 12 very likely now, maybe 90% or more, and the fair value is well above 9.43.
- **Ask:** At 12.0 an informed buyer gains nothing from a settlement of 12. A noise buyer pays above my expected value. So I raise my ask to 12.0 and can safely sell more.
- **Bid:** Buying back would mostly attract informed sellers when die 3 is not 12, and those trades lose money. I put the bid far below the fair value so it is very unlikely to trade.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 12.0}

The settlement value is certain. Die 3 is 12, and neither die 1 nor die 2 can exceed 10, so the contract settles at exactly 12.

An informed counterparty knows this, so I must not quote a bid at or above 12 or an ask at or below 12. Against a noise trader with valuation 12 + N(0, 2.1), a quote at distance d from 12 earns d per fill and fills with probability Φ(-d/2.1). The product d·Φ(-d/2.1) peaks around d ≈ 1.5 at about 0.357 per quote.

My short position doesn't change this, because the settlement value is fixed. I'll quote symmetrically around 12.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 13.5}

The contract is certain to settle at 12. Die 3 is 12, and no other die can exceed 10, so the largest die is 12.

An informed counterparty knows the value is 12. It would never sell to me below 12 or buy from me above 12, so informed traders cannot hurt me on either side if I quote away from 12. Only noise traders matter, and their valuation is 12 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.1.

For a bid at 12 − x, the expected profit is x · P(noise valuation < 12 − x). This is maximised near x ≈ 1.57, which gives a bid of about 10.4. The ask is symmetric, so it goes at about 13.6.

My position of −1 is well inside the ±3 limit, and the settlement value is known, so there is no inventory risk.

{"bid": 10.4, "ask": 13.6}

Fair value of the max of the three dice is about 9.43 before any reveal. Previous trades at 10.3 to 11.9 look like informed buyers, since all three rounds settled at 12, so alpha may be high. I'm quoting wide: ask at 12, where informed buyers have no edge, and bid at 5, where informed sellers can only trade against me if the value is 3 or 4.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 12.0}

Fair value is about 9.4, the mean of the max of the three dice. That figure is the sum of each possible max times its probability, using P(max ≤ x) = F1·F2·F3.

Distribution of the max:

| Max | Probability |
|---|---|
| 12 | 0.333 |
| 10 | 0.25 |
| 9 | 0.167 |
| 8 or less | 0.25 |

The earlier fills point to informed counterparties. They bought at 10.4, 10.3 and 11.9, and all three rounds settled at 12. Updating on that, the posterior for alpha is roughly 0.78 on 0.9, 0.21 on 0.5 and 0.01 on 0.05. That gives an expected alpha of about 0.8.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only profits if the value is above my ask. At 12 the value can never exceed it, so informed traders cannot buy. Noise traders buy about 11% of the time at a good margin. Lowering the ask to around 10 would give informed traders a loss of about 2 each time the value is 12, so I keep the ask at 12.

**Bid:** A bid of 5 loses money in expectation, because an informed seller then hits it when the value is 3 or 4. A bid of 3 cannot be hit by an informed trader, and noise traders almost never sell that low. It costs nothing and keeps a quote on the book.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 12}

Die 3 is 4, so the contract settles at max(die 1, die 2, 4).

Settlement distribution:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 1/12 |
| 5 | 1/6 |
| 6 | 1/8 |
| 8 | 1/8 |
| 9 | 1/8 |
| 10 | 3/8 |

The fair value is about 7.79.

I priced both sides to limit losses to informed traders:
- **Ask:** An ask near 10 loses almost nothing to informed buyers, since the settlement never exceeds 10. A noise trader with valuation above 10 is still fairly likely, roughly a 15% chance. I'll use 9.9.
- **Bid:** A bid of 5 loses only a little to informed sellers, since the settlement is below 5 only when it equals 4. It still catches noise sellers.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 9.9}

Die 3 is 4, so the contract settles at max(die 1, die 2, 4). Enumerating the 24 combinations of die 1 and die 2 gives this distribution for the settlement value:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2/24 |
| 5 | 4/24 |
| 6 | 3/24 |
| 8 | 3/24 |
| 9 | 3/24 |
| 10 | 9/24 |

The mean is about 7.79, so a noise trader's valuation is roughly Normal(7.79, 2.1).

- **Ask:** The settlement can never exceed 10, so an informed trader never buys at an ask of 10.0 or higher. At 10.0 only noise traders buy, which happens about 15% of the time at a profit of about 2.2 each. Lower asks such as 9 or 9.8 lose to informed buyers when the value is 10, so I post 10.0.
- **Bid:** The settlement can never go below 4, so a bid at or below 4 is safe from informed sellers but rarely fills. A bid of 5.0 risks only a small loss to an informed seller when the value is 4, which has probability 2/24. It also fills against noise traders about 9% of the time at a profit of about 2.8, so I post 5.0.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 10.0}

Fair value is about 9.43, the mean of the maximum of the three dice. The maximum is 12 with probability 1/3, 10 with probability 1/4, and 9 with probability about 1/6.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer only buys if the settlement value is above my ask. At 12 an informed buyer never has an edge, since the value cannot exceed 12. Noise traders still buy about 11% of the time at an expected edge of about 2.6. Lower asks like 10.4 lose money to informed buyers when the value is 12, so I ask 12.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers hit low bids when the value is low, and the noise flow is too thin to cover those losses until the bid is around 5. At a bid of 5 the expected profit is roughly breakeven to slightly positive, so I bid 5.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 12}

Fair value is about 9.43, the mean of the largest of the three dice.

- **Ask:** Informed buyers only profit when the value is 12, so an ask just under 12 costs little against them. Noise traders still buy there about 12% of the time, well above fair value. An ask of 11.9 has the best expected profit I found, about +0.13 per quote at the average alpha.
- **Bid:** Against informed sellers, any bid well below fair value loses about as much as noise traders add. A bid of 5 roughly breaks even, and higher bids lose.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 11.9}

Die 3 is 9, so the contract settles at max(9, die 1, die 2). That is 10 if die 1 shows 10 or die 2 shows 10, and 9 otherwise.

- P(neither shows 10) = 5/6 × 3/4 = 0.625, so P(settles at 10) = 0.375.
- The public fair value is 9 × 0.625 + 10 × 0.375 = 9.375.

An informed trader's value is never below 9 and never above 10. A bid of 9 or lower and an ask of 10 or higher therefore cannot be picked off by informed traders, so only noise traders (valuation 9.375 + N(0, 2.1)) will trade.

Expected profit per quote against a noise trader, using the normal tail probabilities:

| Side | Price | Trade probability | Edge per trade | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ask | 10.0 | about 0.38 | 0.625 | about 0.24 |
| Ask | 10.5 | about 0.30 | 1.125 | about 0.33 |
| Ask | 11.0 | about 0.22 | 1.625 | about 0.36 |
| Ask | 11.5 | about 0.16 | 2.125 | about 0.33 |
| Bid | 9.0 | about 0.43 | 0.375 | about 0.16 |
| Bid | 8.0 | about 0.26 | 1.375 | about 0.35 |
| Bid | 7.5 | about 0.19 | 1.875 | about 0.35 |

The best ask is near 11 and the best bid is near 8. I'm quoting slightly inside those, at 8.1 and 10.9.

{"bid": 8.1, "ask": 10.9}

Die 3 is 9, so the contract settles at max(9, die 1, die 2). It settles above 9 only if die 1 or die 2 shows 10.

- P(neither shows 10) = (5/6)(3/4) = 0.625, so the settlement is 9.
- P(at least one shows 10) = 0.375, so the settlement is 10.
- The public fair value is 0.625 × 9 + 0.375 × 10 = 9.375.

**Ask at 10.0:** an informed buyer never trades here, since the settlement is at most 10 and a valuation of 10 is not above an ask of 10. A noise trader buys with probability about 0.38, which is worth about +0.24 × (1 − α) per quote. Lowering the ask to 9.9 exposes me to informed buyers and earns less from noise traders.

**Bid at 9.0:** an informed seller never trades here, since the settlement is at least 9. A noise trader sells with probability about 0.43, earning about 0.375 per trade. Raising the bid to 9.1 lets informed traders sell to me at a loss when the settlement is 9, and it earns less from noise traders.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 10.0}

Fair value is about 9.43, the expected maximum of the three dice. The distribution is skewed: the maximum is 12 with probability 1/3, because die 3 shows 12 on two of its six faces, and it is at least 3 always.

The main risk is informed buyers, so I set the ask where they cannot profit.
- **Ask 12:** An informed trader only buys when the value is strictly above 12, which never happens, so they lose nothing here. Noise traders still buy about 11% of the time, at a profit of roughly 2.6 per unit.
- **Lower asks:** At 11 to 11.8, informed buyers who know the value is 12 take a loss. That loss outweighs the extra noise-trader profit once alpha is high.
- **Bid 3:** The minimum possible settlement is 3, so an informed seller can never trade below it. Noise traders rarely sell this low, but each such trade is profitable.
- **Higher bids:** At 5 to 8, informed sellers who know the value is low cost more than the noise traders earn.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 12}

The fair value of the max of the three dice is about 9.43. The distribution is skewed: the max is 12 with probability 1/3, 10 with 1/4 and 9 with 1/6.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer takes my ask only when the value is 12, so a higher ask costs less against informed flow. At 11.5 the expected loss to informed buyers is about 0.5 × 1/3 per unit of alpha. Noise buyers still pay a large premium over fair value, so the ask stays profitable unless alpha is very high.
- **Bid:** The left tail is thin. At a bid of 5, informed sellers cost little because the value is rarely below 5. Noise sellers, whose valuation is fair value plus Normal(0, 2.1), still sell at that price often enough to leave a small positive edge at moderate alpha.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 11.5}

The settlement value is already certain. Die 3 shows 12, and neither die 1 nor die 2 can exceed 10, so the contract settles at exactly 12.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at exactly 12. I avoid losing to them by keeping the bid at or below 12 and the ask at or above 12.
- **Noise traders:** their valuation is 12 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.1. Quoting x away from 12 earns x per trade, with a trade probability of about 1 − Φ(x/2.1). That expected profit peaks near x ≈ 1.5, at roughly 0.36 per quote.
- **Position:** I'm short 1, so buying at the bid reduces risk. Selling at the ask takes me to -2, which is within the -3 limit.

I'll quote slightly inside that optimum, about 1.4 away on each side.

{"bid": 10.6, "ask": 13.4}

The settlement value is certain. Die 3 is 12, and neither die 1 (max 10) nor die 2 (max 10) can beat it, so the contract settles at exactly 12.

- **Informed traders:** they know the value is 12. They only buy from me if my ask is below 12, and only sell to me if my bid is above 12. Keeping the bid below 12 and the ask at or above 12 means they never trade against me.
- **Noise traders:** their valuation is about 12 plus noise with standard deviation 2.1. A bid d below 12 earns d per fill, with fill probability Φ(−d/2.1). Maximising d·Φ(−d/2.1) puts d at about 0.75 × 2.1 ≈ 1.6. The same holds for the ask, 1.6 above 12.
- **Position:** I'm short 1, so a bid fill is the more useful side. Either side stays within the ±3 limit.

I'll quote 10.4 on the bid and 13.6 on the ask.

The prior probability of heads is 0.5·0.2 + 0.2·0.3 + 0.3·0.5 = 0.31. Over 7 flips that gives 7 × 0.31 = 2.17 expected heads, so an expected settlement of about 10.85.

Settlement values are multiples of 5, and informed counterparties (alpha is 0.48 on average) trade against me whenever the value is on the far side of my quote. A tight spread around 10.85 would lose more to them than it earns from noise traders. A bid of 7 and an ask of 15 gives noise traders enough room to trade at a profit for me, while informed buyers need 4 or more heads to profit at 15.

- **Update from the trade:** the counterparty bought at my ask of 15. That is mildly more likely if the value is high, because an informed buyer needs at least 4 heads to be worth 20 or more, and that is likelier under the 0.5 coin. I nudge my estimate up to about 11.3.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
My estimate of the fair value is about 8.3, below the unconditional 14, so I'm shifting both quotes down.

- **Prior fair value:** the expected heads per flip is 0.35, so 8 flips give 2.8 heads and a value of 14.
- **Information from the last trade:** a counterparty sold to me at 9. That is more likely if the settlement value is low (heads ≤ 1), which is much more likely under the 0.2 coin (P ≈ 0.50) than the 0.5 coin (P ≈ 0.035).
- **Updated estimate:** weighing the chance that the seller was informed against a noise seller, the 0.2 coin now looks about 70–75% likely. That puts fair value near 8.3.
- **Quotes:** I quote about 2 to 4 below and above that fair value to cover adverse selection from informed traders. Being long 1, I lean slightly lower on the bid.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 12}

Flip 1 is heads, so the posterior is P(p=0.5) = 5/7 and P(p=0.2) = 2/7. That gives an expected 2.9 heads in the remaining 7 flips. Total expected heads are 3.9, so fair value is about 19.5. The earlier trades hint slightly lower, since a seller hit my bid of 9 and nothing traded at 6/12. I'm also already long, so I shade my quotes slightly lower and keep a wide spread against informed traders.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 23}

Without any reveal, the fair value is 14. That is 8 flips × 0.35 expected heads per flip × 5.

The settlement distribution is a mixture of the two coins, with mean 14 and values in steps of 5. A noise trader's valuation is roughly 14 + N(0, 7.5).

Since alpha is unknown, I weighed each quote's expected gain from noise traders against its expected loss to informed traders, averaged over alpha ∈ {0.05, 0.5, 0.9}. My rough calculation put the best bid near 5 and the best ask near 23. Quotes tighter than that lose too much to informed traders in the high-alpha case. Quotes much wider give up noise-trader profit.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 23}

My estimate of the contract's fair value is about 12.4. Here is the reasoning.

- **Prior:** each flip has a 0.35 chance of heads, so 8 flips give 2.8 expected heads. At 5 per head, the prior fair value is 14.
- **Alpha:** Round 1 sales at my bids of 9 and 11 came from noise traders. An informed trader knowing the settlement of 20 would not have sold there, and none of them bought my ask of 12 at quote 2. That points to low alpha.
- **Coin:** The sale at 5.5 earlier this round is more likely to come from the low-bias coin, so I put roughly 63% on it. The fair value is then about 0.63 × 8 + 0.37 × 20 ≈ 12.4.
- **Quote:** I quote about 3.5 below and above that fair value. I shade the quote slightly down because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 16}

My fair value estimate is about 17, and I'm quoting around it with a wider spread on the bid side because I'm already long.

- **Flip 1 = 1:** With only the revealed flip, the posterior on the 0.2 coin is 0.2/0.7 ≈ 0.29, so I'd expect about 3.9 heads, or a value near 19.5.
- **Stage-1 trades:** Both counterparties sold to me at low bids (5.5 and 9). That points toward the low-bias coin, since a value of 5 means all remaining flips are tails. alpha is unknown, so I only partly trust this signal. I put the posterior on the 0.2 coin at roughly 0.5.
- **Resulting fair value:** Each remaining flip has probability about 0.35 of heads. That gives 1 + 7 × 0.35 ≈ 3.45 heads, so a fair value near 17.
- **Position:** I'm long +2, so I shade both quotes slightly lower to encourage selling to me less and buying from me more.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 21}

My estimate of the fair value is about 19.

- **Flip 1 = 1:** the posterior on the coin is P(0.2) = 2/7 and P(0.5) = 5/7. That gives an expected 1 + 7 × 0.414 ≈ 3.9 heads, so a value near 19.5.
- **Alpha:** the round 1 trades suggest alpha is probably low. An informed trader with value 20 would have bought at my ask of 19 or 12. Instead, quotes 1, 2 and 4 were handled by noise traders or by nobody.
- **Round 2 sells:** the three sells at 5.5, 9 and 13.5 are mostly noise traders, so they shift the fair value only slightly. I'll use about 19.
- **Quote width:** with noise sd 7.5, the profit-maximising edge is roughly 0.75 × 7.5 ≈ 5.5 from fair on each side.
- **Position skew:** I'm long +3, so I'll shade both sides down a little. That means a slightly lower bid and a slightly tighter ask.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 24}

The public fair value is 5 × 8 × 0.35 = 14, since each flip lands heads with probability 0.35 on average. Informed traders are costly at tight spreads because the settlement value is spread widely, from about 0 to 40. I compared a few spreads by their expected profit per arrival, averaged over the three possible alpha values (0.05, 0.5, 0.9).

| Spread (bid / ask) | Average expected profit per arrival |
|---|---|
| 10 / 18 | negative |
| 7 / 22 | about +0.26 |
| 6 / 24 | about +0.41 |

A wide spread loses little to informed traders and still earns from noise traders, so I'm quoting a bit inside 6 / 24.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 23}

Flip 1 is heads, so the posterior is P(p=0.2) = 2/7 and P(p=0.5) = 5/7. That gives expected remaining heads of 7 × 0.414 ≈ 2.9, so about 3.9 heads in total and a fair value of roughly 19.5.

The stage-1 sells at low bids are only weak evidence about the coin. Past settlements also show that many sellers were noise traders, since they sold below the final value. That suggests alpha is probably not high.

I'm long +2, so I lean slightly toward selling: a somewhat lower bid and an ask just under the 23 that has gone unhit before. The spread is wide enough to protect against informed traders.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 22.5}

Past fills look like noise trades, not informed ones. I sold at bids of 5.5 to 13.5 in rounds 1–3 and the contract settled at 15 or 20 each time, and my ask fill at 22 settled at 20. Informed traders would not have traded on those sides. That points to a low alpha, so I can quote fairly tight.

For a noise-only counterparty with valuation 14 + N(0, 7.5), expected profit per quote is maximised at a half-spread of roughly 5. I widen slightly to 5.5 to allow for some chance of an informed trader.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 19.5}

Fair value is about 17 for this quote. Before any trade this round, the prior gives 8 flips × 0.35 × 5 = 14. The coin is redrawn each round, so earlier settlements say nothing about this round's coin.

The counterparty bought at my ask of 19.5 earlier this round. A buy at that price is much more likely if the coin is the 0.5 coin, which settles around 20, than the 0.2 coin, which settles around 8. Assuming alpha is about 0.5, the probability of the 0.5 coin rises to roughly 0.75, giving a fair value of about 0.75×20 + 0.25×8 ≈ 17.

I'm short one unit, so I lean slightly toward buying. I quote a bid of 13 and an ask of 21.5, a wide spread around 17 to guard against informed traders.

{"bid": 13, "ask": 21.5}

Flip 1 was tails, so the posterior on the P(heads) = 0.2 coin is about 0.615. That gives an expected heads rate of about 0.315 per remaining flip, so the 7 unrevealed flips average about 2.2 heads. That puts fair value near 11.

The earlier buy at 19.5 in this round only nudges that up slightly, since a noise trader with sd 7.5 could easily produce it.

I'm short 1, so I'm happy to lean slightly toward buying. I'm quoting about 3 below and 3 above fair value, to cover the informed-trader risk.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 14.5}

My estimate of fair value is about 11.2. Flip 1 came up tails, so the 0.2-coin has posterior weight 0.8/1.3 ≈ 0.62. That gives an expected heads rate of about 0.315 on the 7 remaining flips, or 5 × 7 × 0.315 ≈ 11.0. The one trade this round, a buy at 19.5, nudges that up slightly.

Settlement is a multiple of 5, so informed traders only profit when the true value is far from my quote. I checked the expected gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders at several quote levels, assuming alpha is around 0.5.

- **Bid:** at 6 the noise gain (about 1.27) slightly exceeds the informed loss (about 1.04). At 7 the loss (about 1.42) exceeds the gain (about 1.2).
- **Ask:** at 15.5 the informed loss (about 1.55) exceeds the noise gain (about 1.22). At 17 the two are roughly balanced (about 1.22 against 1.28).

I am already short 1 unit, which is favourable at my fair value, so I don't need to chase a buy-back. I'll quote slightly wide on both sides.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 16.5}

Before any flips are revealed, the public fair value is 8 flips × 0.35 × 5 = 14. The settlement is bimodal, centred near 8 if the coin has P(heads) = 0.2 and near 20 if it is 0.5. An informed trader therefore usually knows the value is well away from 14. I'm quoting a moderately wide spread around 14 to earn from noise traders without giving too much to informed ones.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 18.5}

Public fair value at this stage is 14, since the expected number of heads is 8 × 0.35 = 2.8 and the contract pays 5 per head. The earlier fills at low bids look like noise traders rather than informed ones, so adverse selection seems modest. I'll quote a moderately tight spread around 14.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 17.5}

Flip 1 = 1 pushes the expected settlement value to about 19.5, since the posterior on the coin is 2/7 for P(heads) = 0.2 and 5/7 for 0.5. The trade I just had shifts that estimate down, and I'm treating the result as only a rough estimate.

- Someone sold to me at 14.5, which an informed seller would only do if the value were 10 or lower. Noise traders also sell there about a quarter of the time.
- Averaging over the three possible alpha values, this pulls my fair value to roughly 15–16.
- This is the last quote of the round, so there is nothing to hedge afterward. I'm keeping a spread around 16 that is wide enough to cover informed-trader risk, with the ask a bit above the fair value and the bid a bit below.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 19.5}

Fair value before any flips is 5 × 8 × 0.35 = 14. Settlement can only be 0, 5, …, 40, and its distribution is skewed: roughly 0.27 chance of 5 or less, and 0.35 chance of 20 or more.

Informed traders pick me off, and alpha is unknown, so I weighed noise-trader edge against informed-trader losses at several quote levels, averaging over alpha ∈ {0.05, 0.5, 0.9}.

- **Ask:** at 17.5 the expected profit is negative, and by about 20 it is roughly break-even. Around 22 it is slightly positive.
- **Bid:** at 8.5 it is slightly negative. Around 6–7 it is positive.

So I quote a bid of 7 and an ask of 22.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 22}

info.raw:

It is also consistent with a noise trader whose valuation happened to be low.

Weighting over the possible values of alpha, the counterparty was informed with probability about 0.57. That puts the fair value near 7.6, and the value is likely 0. Noise valuations are now centred on about 7.6 with a standard deviation of 11.

I'm already long, and a likely-zero value makes buying costly. I'll bid very low, at 1. A noise trader still sells to me often enough at that price, and an informed seller costs me only about 1. I'll ask well above fair, at 22, to limit losses to informed buyers who know the value is high.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 22}

{"bid": 0, "ask": 20}

**Fair value from the flips alone.** After three tails the posterior is about 80% on the 0.2 coin. That gives an expected value of about 5.2.

**What the trades add.** My bids of 5 and 1 were both hit, and my bid of 0 and ask of 20 drew no trade. An informed trader only sells at those bids if the value is 0, so I weighted each alpha and each value by how well it explains the history:
- P(settlement = 0) is about 99%.
- The posterior on alpha leans high: about 73% on 0.9, 24% on 0.5 and 2% on 0.05.

**Bid.** Any bid above 0 is hit by informed sellers, and also by noise sellers, at a loss when the value is about 0. A bid of 0 is never hit by an informed trader, because the value is not strictly below 0. Noise sellers hit it at a small expected gain.

Noise buyers whose valuations run well above the fair value do pay a high price, and the risk of a value of 10 or more is under 1%. Maximizing price times the chance a noise buyer accepts, across the fair-value estimates of about 0.1 and 5.2, puts the best ask at roughly 8–11. I take 9.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 9}

Fair value before any flips is 5 × (0.5 × 0.2 + 0.5 × 0.5) × 10 = 17.5. Round 1 had its own hidden state, so it says nothing about this round's coin.

- **Possible high alpha.** Round 1's three bid hits, even at bids of 5, 1 and 0, make a higher alpha somewhat more likely, so I'm keeping the spread wide.

At these prices, noise traders still trade often enough to pay for the informed losses at alpha around 0.5.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 30}

Fair value is 17.5: the coin's average heads probability is 0.35, so 5 flips give 1.75 expected heads, worth 17.5.

The settlement distribution mixes the two coins. It gives 0 with probability about 0.18, 10 with 0.28, 20 with 0.26, 30 with 0.18, 40 with 0.08 and 50 with 0.02.

The unknown alpha makes wide quotes safer. An informed trader sells to my bid only when the value is 0, and buys from my ask only when the value is 30 or more. Noise traders trade at these levels less often but at better prices for me. Round 1's low-priced sells and the lack of a trade at 7/30 weakly suggest a higher alpha, so I keep the bid low and the ask high.

A bid of 7 and an ask of 29 balance noise-trader edge against informed-trader loss.

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Four dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 7, 10, 11.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 4, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 6, 9, 10, 10.

game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 8 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 8. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.

I set the half-spread by weighing the two effects for each of the three possible alphas (0.05, 0.5, 0.9). A tight spread does well only if alpha is low. At alpha 0.9 it loses heavily to informed traders. A half-spread of about 3 stays positive on average across the three alpha values and limits the informed-trader losses.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 17 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 0, 2 cards worth 5, 3 cards worth 7, 1 card worth 11, 1 card worth 12, 2 cards worth 13, 2 cards worth 14, 4 cards worth 15. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
My estimate of the settlement value is about 23.5 after the first trade. The deck's 17 cards sum to 168, so the prior expected sum of two cards is about 19.8.

The counterparty bought at 22.3. That outcome is likelier when the sum is high, because informed traders buy whenever the sum is above 22.3. About 33% of card pairs sum above 22.3, and those pairs average about 27.4. Weighting by the chance each pair would produce a buy, with alpha at its prior mean of about 0.48, gives an expected sum of roughly 23.5.

I'm short one unit, so I would like to buy back at a reasonable price. Informed traders are a real risk, so I'm keeping the spread fairly wide around 23.5.

{"bid": 21.6, "ask": 25.6}

I'm quoting wide because the counterparty may be informed, and alpha is unknown.

With card 1 = 13, the other 16 cards give these settlement values: 13 (×2), 18 (×2), 20 (×3), 24, 25, 26, 27 (×2) and 28 (×4). The mean is 22.69, which is the public fair value.

I compared quotes by expected profit per quote, using an average alpha of about 0.48 and noise of 4.8:
- **Ask:** it peaks near 28, at about +0.37. At 28, an informed buyer can't profit, and noise traders still buy about 13% of the time at a good margin. Lower asks lose to informed buyers, for example an ask of 24 is negative on average.
- **Bid:** the expected profit is flat at about +0.10 across bids of 15 to 17. I picked 16.5 as a middle point.

{"bid": 16.5, "ask": 28.0}

Card 1 is 13, so the 16 unseen cards sum to 155 and average 9.69. Fair value for the contract is about 22.7. Card 2 would put the settlement at 13, 18, 20, 24, 25, 26, 27 or 28.

- **Ask 28:** no informed buyer can profit, since the maximum settlement is 28. Only noise traders can lift it, and their edge is about 5.3.
- **Bid 16:** an informed seller only hits it if card 2 is 0, which is 2 of 16 cards. Noise sellers pay a larger edge of about 6.7, so the expected value is slightly positive.

I'm keeping the quotes wide because the informed fraction is unknown.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 28}

I'm quoting around a fair value of about 19.76 for this first stage, since nothing is revealed yet.

- **Fair value:** the deck's 17 cards sum to 168, so the mean card is 168/17 ≈ 9.88. Two cards therefore have an expected sum of about 19.76.
- **Spread of outcomes:** the sum has a standard deviation of roughly 6.9.
- **Why a modest spread:** some counterparties may be informed, and they will trade against me when the sum is far from my quote. So I quote about 2.3 on each side of fair value.
- **Noise traders at that width:** with noise of 4.8, a noise trader would still buy at my ask about 31% of the time. The spread should therefore still attract trades from them.

Round 1 gave little information about alpha, so I'm not shading the quote for it.

{"bid": 17.4, "ask": 22.1}

Card 1 is 7, so the settlement is 7 plus card 2, which comes from the remaining 16 cards. Those cards sum to 161, so the fair value is 7 + 161/16 ≈ 17.06.

Counterparties may be informed with unknown alpha, so I quote wide to limit adverse selection:

- **Ask:** I'm long 2, so I'd like to sell. An informed buyer only profits if card 2 is 11 or higher. At 21.8 an informed buyer finds no card worth more than 21.8 (the maximum settlement is 22), so I lose nothing to them. Noise traders still buy sometimes, which gives positive expected value across all alpha cases.
- **Bid:** I'm already long, so I only want a cautious bid well below fair. Informed sellers would hit it when card 2 is 0, giving a settlement of 7. At 10 that costs me about 3 per informed seller with probability 2/16, while noise sellers give a positive edge.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 21.8}

Card 1 is 7, so the remaining 16 cards average about 10.06 and the public fair value of the settlement is about 17.06. I'm at +3, so only the ask is available.

Informed buyers only buy if the settlement value is above my ask. The possible settlement values are 7, 12, 14, 18, 19, 20, 21 or 22. An ask of 22.0 or higher gives informed traders nothing, because the maximum value is 22. Noise traders still buy at 22.0 with probability about 15%, which is roughly 4.9 above fair value. That gives an expected gain of about 0.74 per quote against noise traders and no loss to informed ones.

Asks below 22 pick up a little more noise-trader volume but lose to informed buyers holding a 22. Asks near 18 lose clearly to informed traders. So 22.0 is the safest choice across all possible values of alpha.

{"bid": null, "ask": 22.0}

The informed counterparty's possible settlement values are 14, 19, 21, 25, 26, 27, 28 and 29. They are skewed toward the high end because four of the 16 cards are 15s.

I checked a few quote levels against a mid-range alpha. A tight spread loses too much to informed traders, so I'm quoting wide: the bid sits well below fair value and the ask a little above it, the ask closer in because the 15s weight the upside.

{"bid": 19.5, "ask": 26.5}

The settlement value could be 14, 19, 21, 25, 26, 27, 28 or 29. A wide spread guards against informed traders, who know the exact value. A tight quote loses about 2 to 3 per trade to them. I tested several ask and bid levels against both counterparty types, taking alpha = 0.5 as a middle case:

{"bid": 17.3, "ask": 21.7}

I'm long +2, so I'd like to sell and don't need to buy more.

- **Ask:** At 26.5, only an informed buyer holding a 27 (4 of 16 cards) trades against me, and my loss there is just 0.5. A noise buyer pays about 4.75 above fair value and trades roughly 16% of the time. This is positive across the alpha values I can't rule out.
- **Bid:** I set it well below fair value. An informed seller with a 12 or 17 would hit a higher bid at a loss to me. At 14.5 only the two 12-cards (value 12) can hit an informed sale, and noise sellers pay me a large edge when they do trade.

{"bid": 14.5, "ask": 26.5}

My position is 0, so both sides are available.

{"bid": 12.9, "ask": 28}

- **Ask:** 28 is the top possible settlement, so an informed buyer can never profit against it. Only noise traders can lift it. That makes 28 the best ask, with an expected profit of about 0.37 per quote averaged over the three alpha values.

{"bid": 13.0, "ask": 28.0}

- **Ask:** A low ask is picked off by informed buyers when the hidden card is 13–15, so I set it high, near 27. At 27 no informed buyer gains, and noise traders still buy about 14% of the time at a gain of about 5 each.
- **Bid:** A bid near 17.8 gains about 0.2 per quote on average. It also helps cover my short position of -2. A higher bid loses too much to informed sellers holding a 12, 17 or 19.

{"bid": 17.8, "ask": 27}

**Bid:** A bid near 12 to 13 can only lose a little to an informed seller, since the lowest settlement is 12. It earns a large margin of about 9 whenever a noise trader sells. Higher bids give up more to informed sellers at 12 and 17.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.1 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.6 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The unconditional mean is 7 × (0.4×0.1 + 0.3×0.2 + 0.3×0.6) = 1.96 heads. Informed counterparties are a real risk, especially on the ask. The contract can settle well above 1.96 if the 0.6 coin was picked, so I quote a wide, asymmetric spread around fair value.

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 3.3}

Before any flips are revealed, the public fair value is the prior mean of the heads count: 7 × (0.4·0.1 + 0.3·0.2 + 0.3·0.6) = 7 × 0.28 = 1.96.

The settlement distribution is right-skewed, which makes informed buyers costly on my ask. It works out to P(0) ≈ 0.25, P(1) ≈ 0.26, P(2) ≈ 0.16, P(3) ≈ 0.10, P(4) ≈ 0.10, P(5) ≈ 0.08, P(6) ≈ 0.04 and P(7) ≈ 0.01.

- **Ask:** At 3.3, an informed buyer only trades when the value is 4 or more, which has probability about 0.22 and an average value near 4.8. At alpha around 0.5 that loss outweighs the profit from noise buyers, so I keep the ask wide.
- **Bid:** Around 0.8–0.9, an informed seller only trades when the value is 0, which costs me less than I gain from noise sellers. This side is roughly break-even to slightly positive.

I'll keep the quotes close to last round's, with a slightly higher bid and a slightly wider ask.

{"bid": 0.9, "ask": 3.4}

Before any flips are revealed, the public fair value is 7 × (0.4·0.1 + 0.3·0.2 + 0.3·0.6) = 7 × 0.28 = 1.96.

The settlement distribution is skewed. The 0.6 coin gives a mean of 4.2, so an informed buyer is dangerous on the ask side. The 0.1 and 0.2 coins mostly settle at 0 to 1, so an informed seller is dangerous on the bid side.

I'll quote asymmetrically around 1.96 with a wider ask:

- **Ask 3.0:** Noise traders buy about 21% of the time. An informed buyer needs a settlement of at least 4, which happens about 22% of the time, usually at around 4.7.
- **Bid 1.1:** This is well below fair value, so a seller who trades is giving me some edge, and an informed seller (settlement at most 1) is only a moderate risk.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 3.0}

The two revealed flips (0 then 1) update the coin's bias, which gives the fair value for the contract.

**Posterior over the coin.** The likelihood of tails then heads is p(1−p) for each coin.

| P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood | Prior × likelihood |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 0.4 | 0.09 | 0.036 |
| 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.16 | 0.048 |
| 0.6 | 0.3 | 0.24 | 0.072 |

The weights sum to 0.156, so the posterior mean of p is 0.0564 / 0.156 ≈ 0.36.

**Fair value.** One head is already revealed, and the 5 unrevealed flips contribute 5 × 0.36 ≈ 1.8 more. Fair value is about 1 + 1.8 = 2.8. The earlier sale at my bid of 1.1 in stage 1 is only weak evidence, so I tilt the estimate down slightly.

**Quotes.** Informed counterparties are possible and the remaining uncertainty is wide, so I keep a wide spread around 2.8. I'm long +1, so I shade the ask down a little to make selling more likely and bring my position back toward flat.

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.1 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.6 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.

info.raw:
The fair value is 11.9, from 7 flips at an average heads probability of 0.34, times 5. The settlement value is skewed: the 0.1 coin comes up half the time, so low outcomes are common. I priced both sides with a quick expected-profit comparison, averaging over the three possible alpha values.

- **Ask:** at any ask near fair, informed buyers cost more than noise traders pay. Profit per sale turns roughly break-even only around 25, so I quote there.
- **Bid:** informed sellers only hurt when the value is 0, which has probability about 0.24. Noise traders sell often enough at a very low bid for this to be profitable on average, so I bid 1.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 25.0}

My fair value for the contract is 11.9. That is 5 × 7 × 0.34, where 0.34 = 0.5×0.1 + 0.1×0.5 + 0.4×0.6 is the expected heads probability.

The distribution of the settlement value is skewed. The 0.1 coin gives a mean of about 3.5 and the 0.6 coin gives a mean of about 21. An informed trader would therefore buy from me when the 0.6 coin is likely and sell to me when the 0.1 coin is likely.

My first quote of 1/25 drew no trade, so I'm tightening to a moderate spread around 11.9. The spread stays wide enough to cover the adverse-selection loss against informed counterparties.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 15.5}

Posterior on the coin after flips 0, 0, 1 (one head, two tails):

| Coin P(heads) | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 0.0405 | 0.443 |
| 0.5 | 0.0125 | 0.137 |
| 0.6 | 0.0384 | 0.420 |

The expected heads rate for the remaining 4 flips is about 0.365, so the expected settlement is 5 × (1 + 4 × 0.365) ≈ 12.3.

The settlement value is 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25, depending on how many of the remaining 4 flips are heads, with probabilities of roughly 0.31, 0.23, 0.22, 0.18 and 0.06.

The informed share is unknown, so I use its average of about 0.48. For each candidate price I compare the noise-trader profit, weighted by 1 − α, against the informed-trader loss, weighted by α.

- **Ask:** the expected profit per quote peaks around 20, where it is about +0.39. At 15 it is about −0.25, because informed buyers take too much.
- **Bid:** the best bid is 5, the lowest possible settlement. Informed sellers can never gain there, and the expected profit is about +0.56.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 20}

I set fair value at the unconditional mean. The mean heads probability is 0.5·0.1 + 0.1·0.5 + 0.4·0.6 = 0.34, so expected heads are 7 × 0.34 = 2.38 and the contract's expected settlement is 11.9. Round 1's coin doesn't carry over, because a new state is drawn each round.

The round 1 history favours a lower alpha. My quote of 8.5/15.5 got no trade even though the settlement of 5 meant an informed trader would have sold to me. That points to a noise trader, who would not trade at those prices about 38% of the time. Weighting that evidence, I put roughly 52% on alpha = 0.05, 38% on 0.5 and 10% on 0.9, so the expected alpha is about 0.3.

I compared expected profit per quote, mixing noise and informed traders at that alpha, for several symmetric-ish spreads:

| Bid / ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 8 / 16 | about 0 |
| 6 / 18 | about +0.5 |
| 4 / 20 | about +0.7 |
| 2 / 22 | about +0.6 |

The best spread is around 4 / 20, so I'm quoting that.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 20}

My estimate of the fair value is about 16.5, so I'm quoting around it with a wide spread. The adverse-selection risk is high because alpha is unknown.

- **Prior value:** the mean heads probability is 0.5×0.1 + 0.1×0.5 + 0.4×0.6 = 0.34. That gives 7 × 0.34 × 5 = 11.9.
- **Update from the trade:** a counterparty bought at 20 in quote 1 of this round. That is more likely if the coin is biased toward heads, so I shifted weight to the 0.6 coin. A rough posterior is about 68% on the 0.6 coin, 11% on the 0.5 coin and 21% on the 0.1 coin. The implied mean heads probability is about 0.485, which gives a value near 17.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 21}

I estimate the settlement value at about 21–22, and I'm quoting a bid and ask roughly 3 below and 4 above that.

{"bid": 18.5, "ask": 25.5}

**Posterior on the coin** (prior × likelihood of HHT, p²(1−p)):

- p = 0.5: 0.1 × 0.125 = 0.0125
- p = 0.6: 0.4 × 0.144 = 0.0576

These sum to 0.0746, so the posterior is about 6.0%, 16.8% and 77.2%. That gives E[p] ≈ 0.553.

**Fair value:** 2 heads are already in, and the 4 remaining flips add 4 × 0.553 ≈ 2.21 expected heads. So the settlement value is about 5 × (2 + 2.21) ≈ 21.1.

**Adverse selection:** The earlier trades in this round are contradictory. game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 6 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 6. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The first two draws were both blue, so I need the posterior on the number of red balls R.

**Posterior on R.** The likelihood of two blue draws is (6−R)(5−R)/30. With the uniform prior this gives relative weights 30, 20, 12, 6, 2, 0, 0 for R = 0 to 6, out of 70. So E[R] = 1 and the public fair value is 10. The settlement value V is 0, 10, 20, 30 or 40 with probabilities of about 43%, 29%, 17%, 9% and 3%.

**Bid.** V is never below 0, so a bid of 0 can't lose money on any trade. An informed seller would need a valuation below 0, which never happens. Only noise traders trade there, and they sell when their valuation falls below 0. That happens with probability about 24% and earns about 10 per fill on average. Raising the bid to 1 or 2 exposes me to informed sellers when V = 0, and the expected profit averaged over alpha comes out lower.

**Ask.** I compared asks across the three possible alphas, averaging the loss to informed buyers against the gain from noise buyers. Expected profit rises from about 0.0 at an ask of 17 to about 0.54 at 20, then flattens near 0.68 for asks between 24 and 28. An ask of 25 sits in that flat region.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 25}

The two blue draws leave 0 to 4 red balls, and the posterior mean count is 1. The public fair value is therefore about 10.

**Posterior.** The weight on k red balls is proportional to C(6−k, 2). That gives weights 30, 20, 12, 6, 2 for k = 0 to 4 (total 70). The settlement value is 0, 10, 20, 30 or 40 with those weights, and its mean is 10.

**Ask.** Noise traders have valuation N(10, 14). An informed buyer only takes the ask when the value is above it, which costs me money. I compared asks assuming the average alpha of about 0.48.
- At 15 and 20, informed losses outweigh the noise-trader edge, so expected profit is negative or small.
- At 25 the expected profit is about +0.69 per quote.
- Asks of 28 and 30 earn about 0.68 and 0.65, so the profit curve is flat. I'll quote 25.

**Bid.** An informed seller only trades when the value is 0, and at a bid of 0 an informed trader whose valuation is exactly 0 does not sell. A bid of 0 therefore faces no informed losses and still catches noise sellers (valuation below 0) with probability about 0.24, for about +1.24. Higher bids lose money to informed sellers at a value of 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 25}

I quote symmetrically around the public fair value, which is 30 before any draws are revealed (the number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 6, so the mean is 3 and the settlement mean is 30).

Informed traders know the value, which is one of 0, 10, ..., 60. I compared expected profit per quote at several half-spreads, averaging over the three possible alpha values (mean about 0.48).

| Half-spread | Bid / ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 20 / 40 | about -1.7 (negative) |
| 20 | 10 / 50 | about +0.2 |
| 25 | 5 / 55 | about +0.3 |
| 29-30 | about 1 / 59 | about +0.4 to +0.5 |

Tight quotes lose to informed traders, while noise traders (standard deviation 14) rarely trade at wide prices. The edge is therefore small and best at a very wide spread. I'll quote near the extremes.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 58}

I set the public fair value at 30, since the number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 6 (mean 3) and nothing has been revealed this round.

Informed traders know the settlement value exactly, so a tight spread loses to them. Noise traders value the contract at 30 plus Normal(0, 14) noise, so a wide spread earns little from them. Since alpha is unknown, I compared expected profit per quote across spreads, averaging over alpha = 0.05, 0.5 and 0.9.

- A spread of 20/40 has negative expected profit once alpha is 0.5 or higher.
- Spreads of 8/52 and 5/55 are modestly positive on average.
- Wider spreads still look slightly better, because the losses to informed traders shrink faster than the noise-trader gains.

I'll quote 4/56, a little tighter than the very widest spreads, so I still have some chance of a trade and of learning about alpha.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 56}

Two blue draws leave a posterior over the red count k of 30/70 for k=0, 20/70 for k=1, 12/70 for k=2, 6/70 for k=3 and 2/70 for k=4. That gives a fair value of about 10 and a settlement distribution skewed toward 0.

- **Bid:** A bid of 0 can only fill against noise traders, because an informed seller can't profit when the value is at least 0. It earns about 2.4 per noise-trader arrival. Any higher bid exposes me to informed sellers when the value is 0, which has probability about 43%.
- **Ask:** Comparing expected profit averaged over alpha, asks of 22 to 28 come out about equal. An ask of 25 balances noise-trader profit against losses to informed buyers.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 25}

The first two draws were blue, so I'm updating the number of red balls R. Since P(first two blue | R) is proportional to (6−R)(5−R), the weights for R = 0 to 4 are 30, 20, 12, 6, 2, and R = 5 or 6 are ruled out. That gives E[R] = 1, so the public fair value is about 10. The settlement value is likely 0, 10 or 20 (about 43%, 29% and 17%).

**Bid:** At a bid of 0, noise traders sell to me whenever their valuation is below 0, which happens about 24% of the time and earns about 10 each time. An informed seller can only get 0 from me, so there's no adverse selection cost. Raising the bid adds informed-seller losses without much extra noise-trader gain.

**Ask:** I compared asks of 22, 25 and 30, averaging over the three possible values of alpha. An ask of 25 gives the best balance of noise-trader profit against losses to informed buyers, who only pay it when the value is 30 or 40.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 25}

I quote around the stage-1 fair value of 30 (6 red balls at 10 each, with the red count uniform on 0–6), and I put the quotes wide.

- **Informed traders:** the settlement value is one of 0, 10, ..., 60, each equally likely. An informed trader only trades when it beats my price, so tighter quotes lose more to them.
- **Noise traders:** their valuation is about N(30, 14), so wide quotes rarely trade, but each trade earns a large edge.

I compared symmetric spreads around 30 and averaged over the three possible alpha values (0.05, 0.5, 0.9):

| Half-spread | Quotes | Approx. expected profit per quote |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 20 / 40 | clearly negative |
| 15 | 15 / 45 | about -0.56 |
| 20 | 10 / 50 | about +0.2 |
| 25 | 5 / 55 | about +0.27 |

Only the widest spreads come out positive, so I pick a half-spread of 24, between the last two rows.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 54}

Before any draws are revealed, the public fair value is 30, the mean of 10 × a red count that is uniform on 0 to 6. Noise traders value the contract at about 30 with a standard deviation of 14.

Nine quotes with no trades suggest alpha is probably low, since a high-alpha informed trader would likely have hit one of my wide quotes. So I can tighten somewhat. I can't go too tight, though, because informed traders win a lot when the value is 0, 10, 50 or 60.

A spread of about ±12 around 30 balances the noise-trader edge against the informed-trader losses. Under my rough posterior on alpha, ±10 and ±14 give about the same expected profit.

{"bid": 18, "ask": 42}

Draws 1 and 2 are both blue, so I update the prior on the number of red balls R. R is uniform on 0 to 6, and the chance that the first two draws are blue is proportional to (6−R)(5−R). That gives weights 30, 20, 12, 6, 2, 0, 0 for R = 0 to 6, which sum to 70.

The expected R is (0·30 + 1·20 + 2·12 + 3·6 + 4·2) / 70 = 1. The public fair value is therefore 10. The settlement values are 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 with probabilities 30/70, 20/70, 12/70, 6/70 and 2/70.

Noise traders value the contract at 10 plus Normal(0, 14) noise. I use alpha ≈ 0.48, the average of the three possible values.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only takes it when the value is above the ask, so asks of 25 to 30 lose little to them. Against noise buyers the expected margin is ask − 10. By my estimate the expected profit peaks near an ask of 27, where noise buyers contribute about +1.0 and informed buyers cost about −0.30. That nets about +0.70 per quote.

**Bid:** A bid of 0 is never hit by an informed seller, because the lowest possible value is 0 and a valuation must be strictly below the bid. Noise sellers still hit it about 24% of the time at an expected gain of 10. That is worth about +1.24, which beats higher bids, since informed sellers at value 0 would cost money there.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 27}

Draws 1 and 2 were both blue. Weighting each red count R (0 to 6) by the chance of that outcome, C(6−R,2)/C(6,2), gives relative weights 15, 10, 6, 3, 1, 0, 0. These sum to 35, so the posterior mean of R is 1 and the public fair value is 10.

An informed trader would then know the settlement value is 0, 10, 20, 30 or 40, with probabilities of about 0.43, 0.29, 0.17, 0.09 and 0.03.

- **Ask:** I compared expected profit per quote at several asks, assuming alpha of about 0.5. It peaks at an ask of about 26, because noise traders still buy there often enough to outweigh the loss to informed buyers at 30 and 40.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers can only hit a bid if the value is below it, and the value of 0 is the lowest possible. A bid of 0 is therefore never picked off by an informed trader, while still earning from noise sellers. Raising the bid to 1 or more adds informed losses that outweigh the extra fills.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 26}

With no draws revealed, the public fair value is 3 red balls × 10 = 30. The settlement value is uniform on {0, 10, …, 60}.

I priced symmetric quotes around 30, using a mean alpha of about 0.48 (the average of the three possible values). An informed trader costs me money whenever the value lies outside my quotes, so I compared the noise-trader gains against the informed losses at each spread:

- A spread of ±10 to ±15 loses money on average, because informed traders take the 50 and 60 outcomes.
- At ±25 to ±29 the expected profit is slightly positive, because informed traders can only profit on the value 60 (or 0). It rises to about +0.5 per quote at ±30.

The edge is small everywhere, so I take a wide quote that is nearly immune to informed traders but still catches the occasional noise trade.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 59}

With no information yet, the contract's fair value is 30, since the number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 6 and the value is 10 times that count. A noise trader's valuation is about Normal(30, 14), and an informed trader knows the value, which is one of 0, 10, ..., 60.

I compared symmetric spreads around 30 and averaged over the three possible alpha values:

- **Spread of 10 (bid 20, ask 40):** expected profit is negative, about -0.8 per side, because informed traders take the 50 and 60 outcomes from me.
- **Spread of 20 to 25:** roughly break-even, about +0.1 per side.
- **Spread of about 29 to 30 (bid near 0, ask near 60):** best, about +0.2 to +0.25 per side, because informed traders can barely profit while noise traders still occasionally trade.

The history doesn't justify tightening. The settlement was 20 in every round, so informed traders had no reason to trade at my earlier quotes. The lack of trades says little about alpha, and if anything it leans slightly toward high alpha, since only noise traders would have traded. I'll keep the wide quote.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 59}

With draw 1 = 0 and draw 2 = 1, the number of red balls R can only be 1 to 5. Weighting each R by the chance of seeing a blue then a red, (6−R)/6 × R/5, gives weights 5, 8, 9, 8, 5 out of 35.

The settlement value is 10×R, so the expected value is 30. Its distribution is:

| Settlement | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 5/35 | 8/35 | 9/35 | 8/35 | 5/35 |

The settlement value cannot go below 10 or above 50 here, so an informed trader can't profit from a bid at 12 or an ask at 48 by much. Noise traders (valuation = 30 + Normal(0, 14)) still hit those prices fairly often.

I compared symmetric quotes around 30 with half-spread d, taking the average informed probability as about 0.48:
- **d = 5:** expected value is negative, since informed traders take too much.
- **d = 10:** about +0.55 per side.
- **d = 17 to 20:** about +0.78 to +0.8 per side, the best range.

I'm using d = 18, which gives a bid of 12 and an ask of 48.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 48}

With draw 1 = 0 and draw 2 = 1, the posterior over the number of red balls is proportional to (6−r)·r for r = 1 to 5, which gives a mean of 3 red balls, a value of 30.

My last fill, a sale to me at 12, is informative. Only an informed seller who knows r = 1 (value 10) would sell below 12, and a noise trader sells there only about 10% of the time. That pushes the posterior toward r = 1, giving about a 64% chance the value is 10. The fair value drops to roughly 18.5. The same fill also makes a high alpha more likely.

- **Bid:** A bid of 10 earns about 8.5 per noise sale. A value-10 informed seller sells at 10 for no loss. Bidding 11 or higher exposes me to losses from informed sellers.
- **Ask:** Asks below about 35 lose to informed buyers who know the value is 30 or more. An ask of 40 balances that loss against the gain from noise buyers.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 40}

Before any draws are revealed, the red count is uniform on 0 to 6, so the fair value is 30. The settlement value is one of 0, 10, ..., 60, each with probability 1/7.

I compared a few ask levels, treating the bid as the mirror image.

- **Ask 45:** about −0.35 per quote on average over alpha, so the adverse selection from informed buyers outweighs the noise-trader gain.
- **Ask 50:** about +0.16 per quote. An informed buyer only profits at value 60 (a 10 loss to me at 1/7 probability, about −1.43). A noise trader buys with probability about 0.077 at an average edge of about 23, about +1.77.
- **Ask 52:** about +0.15 per quote, essentially the same as 50.
- **Ask 55:** about +0.1 per quote, with less volume.

I'll quote 10 / 50, symmetric around 30 near the optimum.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 50}

I priced each side by weighing noise-trader flow against informed flow. Noise traders' valuations are 30 plus Normal noise with sd 14. Informed traders know the settlement value, which is uniform on {0, 10, ..., 60}. Alpha is unknown, so I used its average of about 0.48.

- **Bid around 10–12:** edge is roughly break-even to slightly positive. Raising the bid to 15 or 20 turns it negative, because informed sellers with a value of 0 or 10 cost more than the extra noise-trader flow earns.
- **Ask:** the same logic mirrored around 30 puts the ask near 48–50. I'm already long one unit, so I shade it slightly lower to 47. That makes a sale a little more likely without adding much adverse-selection risk.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 47}

The likelihood of two blues is proportional to (6−R)(5−R), and with the uniform prior this gives weights of 30, 20, 12, 6 and 2 out of 70 for R = 0 to 4. The expected R is 1, so the fair value is about 10. The settlement value is 0, 10, 20, 30 or 40 with those probabilities.

I'm already long 2 units, bought at 10 each, so I want to be more cautious on the bid than on the ask.

- **Bid:** An informed seller with value 0 (3/7 chance) hits any bid above 0. A low bid of about 4 still earns on noise sellers, since fair value is 10, without taking too much adverse selection. It also keeps me from getting much longer.
- **Ask:** Informed buyers only trade when the value is 20 or more. Asks of 24 to 26 lose the least to them, and noise traders still buy at a good margin. An ask of 24 gives a positive expected edge and helps reduce my long position.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 24}

Draws 1 and 2 are both blue, so the posterior on the number of red balls R is proportional to 15, 10, 6, 3, 1 for R = 0 to 4. That puts the fair value near 10.

I'm long 3, so only the ask is allowed, and selling above fair value gains the difference against what I hold. The ask trades against two kinds of counterparty:

- **Noise traders** buy when their valuation (10 plus noise with sd 14) exceeds my ask. A higher ask earns more per trade but trades less often.
- **Informed traders** buy only when the settlement value is above my ask, which costs me. The cost shrinks as the ask rises.

Weighting the two with an average alpha of about 0.48, the expected edge is roughly flat across asks of 24 to 27, at about 0.7 per quote. At 20 it is lower, at about 0.56, and at 16 or below it turns negative. I'll take 25.

{"bid": null, "ask": 25}

With no draws revealed yet, the public fair value is the prior mean of 30 (the red count is uniform over 0 to 6, so the settlement value is uniform over 0, 10, ..., 60).

Quoting tight around 30 loses money against informed traders. At an ask of 45, an informed buyer takes an average loss of about 2.9 per quote when the value is 50 or 60. A noise trader pays about 2.1 per quote in expected gain. That is only profitable if alpha is below roughly 0.43. Averaged over the three possible alphas, a 45 ask has negative expected value. The bid side is the mirror image.

Quotes around 8 and 52 sit near break-even on average. They earn a little if alpha is low and lose little if it is high. I'm keeping the wide quotes from round 1.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 52}

The buy at my 52 ask is strong evidence the value is high. Earlier rounds suggest a high share of informed traders. Informed buyers only lift an ask of 52 when the value is 60, which means all 6 balls are red. I put the chance of 60 at roughly 90%, so my fair value estimate is about 57.

- **Ask 62:** this is above the maximum possible value of 60, so an informed trader never buys it. A noise trader who does buy gives me a positive expected edge, since I estimate fair value near 57.
- **Bid 54:** buying here is below my 57 estimate and would cover my short. Informed sellers only hit it if the value is at most 50, which is unlikely given the evidence.

{"bid": 54, "ask": 62}

With draws 1 and 2 both red, the posterior on the red count k puts most weight on high values. The prior is uniform on 0 to 6, so the weights are proportional to k(k−1), giving k=6 about 43% and k=5 about 29%. That makes the fair value about 50.

The earlier trades sharpen this further:
- My ask of 52 was bought in stage 1. A noise trader would do that only about 6% of the time, so it points toward an informed buyer who knows the value is 60.
- Counterparties also traded against my quotes repeatedly in rounds 4 and 5, which fits a high alpha.
- Weighting over alpha, I put P(k=6) at roughly 0.95, so the settlement value is most likely 60.

Pricing the quotes on that basis:
- **Ask:** the maximum settlement value is 60, so an informed trader never buys above 60. Only noise traders buy at a high ask. I'll ask 70, which should give a good expected edge per fill, and a fill takes me to -3, which is allowed.
- **Bid:** an informed trader with value around 60 never sells to me, so only noise traders hit the bid. A bid around 48 should earn a solid edge against an expected value near 59 when it fills, and buying back would also reduce my short.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 70}

**Posterior.** Draws 1 and 2 were both red. The likelihood of that for k red balls is proportional to k(k−1). The posterior weights for k = 2 through 6 are therefore 2, 6, 12, 20 and 30, out of 70. Settlement values are 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60, so the expected value is 50.

**Ask.** The maximum possible settlement is 60, so an informed buyer never pays more than 60. Below 60, informed buyers win the trade in the k = 6 case.
